name: Clematis

project_scope.selection_mode: four canonical learner concepts; native-range tags kept separate
project_scope.note: Four installed learner cards. C. texensis meets existing three-county native PASS; drummondii and pitcheri are Texas natives but their earlier target-zone PASS erroneously counted out-of-zone Williamson, and are currently UNRESOLVED with 2 approved counties each; C. terniflora is introduced NON_NATIVE_COMPARISON.

shared_traits: woody or perennial climbing vines with opposite leaves
petal-like sepals rather than true petals
achenes often bearing persistent elongated styles/beaks
priority: length and plumosity of achene beaks
study_strategy.warning: Do not identify leatherflowers by color alone; sepal margin architecture and fruit beaks are critical.
study_strategy.look_here_first: Verify opposite leaves on a vine, then find ONE flower/fruit cluster. Open four-sepal flowers: compare native dioecious C. drummondii and introduced many-flowered C. terniflora. Nodding leathery urn-shaped flowers: compare C. pitcheri and C. texensis by the edge of a SEPAl, not just flower color. Later inspect an actual seedhead: plumose long beaks versus short appressed-haired beaks.
photo_teaching_order: opposite leaf node, leaflet attachment and climbing leaf stalk
open vs urn flower side views
hairy edge and rolled tip of four sepals in pitcheri / thick noncrispate margins in texensis
seedhead showing individual achene, persistent style and plumose hairs
paired leaves for drummondii versus terniflora

quick_key.if: Open pale flowers, often male/female flowers on different plants; leaflets divided/lobed; later a mass of VERY long silvery feathery achene tails
quick_key.then: Clematis drummondii — native old man's beard

quick_key.if: Open white/cream small flowers in large branched MANY-flowered sprays; opposite mostly 3–5 leaflets with smooth, ENTIRE edges
quick_key.then: Clematis terniflora — introduced sweet autumn clematis; native-only tally excluded

quick_key.if: Nodding leathery urn, four thick but distally THIN EXPANDED/CRISPATE sepal margins with recurved points; mature seed beaks ~1–3 cm little-appressed-hairy
Nodding leathery urn, unexpanded THICK noncrispate sepal margins and recurved points; mature seed beaks 4–7 cm PLUMOSE

shared_genus_characters.look_here_first: Confirm a climbing vine with opposite leaves, then inspect the flower: the showy parts are sepals, not petals. Use mature sepal shape and the later achene head for species-level work.
shared_genus_characters.shared: Project Clematis are climbing perennials with opposite leaves, petaloid sepals, numerous stamens and pistils, and aggregate achenes with persistent styles.

overlap_and_cautions: Flower color is secondary; inspect sepal margins and tips.
Opposite divided leaves establish the genus but do not reliably separate these species.
Use mature fruit for achene-beak comparisons.
If a mature sepal edge is not visible, keep a leatherflower ID provisional.

realistic_lookalikes.separate_by: Require Clematis reproductive architecture: petaloid sepals, many free stamens and pistils, then aggregate achenes with persistent styles.

diagnostic_photo_checklist.purpose: Show open flower versus urn and expose the sepal tips.
Show expanded/crispate/recurved versus non-expanded sepal margins.
Compare persistent style/beak length and plumosity.

diagnostic_review_handoffs: If mature sepal-tip structure cannot be verified, request a targeted flower-side macro rather than forcing the species ID.
Any species outside the current three-species project set goes to Taxonomy + Diagnostic Review before scope changes.

comparison_cards.title: Native old man's beard vs introduced sweet autumn clematis
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Not all white Clematis are the same: count flowers on a branch, then look at individual compound LEAFLETS (deeply divided/lobed in drummondii vs mostly entire and oval in terniflora). On drummondii separate male/female vines; on terniflora flowers mostly bisexual. Both can develop fluffy seed structures.
photo_requirements: leaf blade edge closeups at the same scale
individual male/female flowers versus bisexual bloom
mature seedhead with single fruit beak
comparison_cards.caution: Do not identify merely from fluffy silver seedheads; both produce plumed styles.

comparison_cards.title: Purple versus scarlet leatherflowers
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Find one sepAl EDGE near the tip: pitcheri = narrowly expanded thin CRISPATE margin, texensis = thick not expanded not crispate. Later verify fruit: pitcheri ~1–3 cm weakly hairy beak vs texensis 4–7 cm plumose beak.
photo_requirements: matched lateral urns at same scale
high resolution sepal edge macro arrows (true sepal margin not a petal)
two ripe achenes with cm ruler
comparison_cards.caution: Purple-versus-red hue is not a sufficient diagnosis in intermediate cultivated flowers; need wild species concept and sepal/fruit structure.

comparison_cards.title: Leatherflower or open-flowered clematis?
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Clematis has no true petals: the colored flower parts are four SEPALS. In the leatherflowers they join visually into a nodding urn; in drummondii and terniflora they spread openly.
photo_requirements: label sepals, stamens and central female parts

photo_priority: paired exact sepal margins pitcheri vs texensis
single female flower C drummondii, distinct from male
paired mature leatherflower achenes with rulers

look_here_first: First inspect the FLOWER, then a LEAF STALK and mature FRUIT. Four spreading petal-like SEPALS and open blooms: old man's beard C. drummondii (often lobed leaflets, male/female flowers on different vines) versus introduced sweet autumn C. terniflora (many small white flowers, usually entire leaflets). Four SEPALS arranged as a nodding leathery URN: C. pitcheri versus C. texensis. Their definitive distinction is SEPAl-MARGIN texture and later ACHENE-BEAK hair/length, not simply purple versus red color.

genus_diagnostics.flower: The showy units are normally FOUR SEPALS, not petals. In this learner C. drummondii and introduced C. terniflora have spreading OPEN flowers; C. pitcheri and C. texensis have leathery nodding URNS made from four closely arranged sepals. Many separate stamens and pistils belong to the buttercup-family reproductive plan.
genus_diagnostics.leaves: Inspect opposite leaves and individually divided leaflets. C. drummondii often has deeply lobed/cut leaflets; C. terniflora generally has relatively entire-edged leaflets. C. pitcheri and C. texensis can vary greatly in leaflet shape; leaf outline alone does not settle their identity.
genus_diagnostics.stem: Trace a climbing LEAF STALK: petioles/petiolules wind around supports. They are not independent tendrils and not rootlets like those of trumpet creeper. A node macro is useful to see opposite attachment.
genus_diagnostics.inflorescence: Compare one whole flowering shoot, not just one bloom: C. terniflora often makes broad many-flowered sprays; C. drummondii has fewer, more widely separated open blooms. Leatherflower blooms are usually nodding and borne singly or in small groups from leaf axils.
genus_diagnostics.fruit: Look for MANY individual dry ACHENES in a head, each bearing the persistent style or beak. C. drummondii produces especially long feathery styles; C. terniflora can also make feathery seedheads. Pitcheri fruit beaks about 1–3 cm, usually relatively short/sparsely hairy; texensis about 4–7 cm, conspicuously PLUMOSE. Mature matched photos needed.
genus_diagnostics.sepal: For the two leatherflowers, inspect the very EDGE of a mature floral SEPAL close to its recurved tip. C. pitcheri margins become narrowly expanded, thin and crispate (wavy/ruffled), whereas C. texensis has thick unexpanded, noncrispate margins. Flowers need matched magnification, a clear edge, and real verified arrows.

shared_traits: woody or perennial climbing vines with opposite leaves
petal-like sepals rather than true petals
achenes often bearing persistent elongated styles/beaks
Climb with winding PETIOLES/PETIOLULES (leaf stalks), not true independent tendrils; species vary in foliage and flower architecture.
high_value_diagnostics: Spot the showy SEPALS rather than calling them petals.
Open spreading flower vs nodding leathery urn separates the two local teaching groups.
For white/open flowers, compare entire versus cut leaflets and wide multi-flower panicles.
For leatherflowers, check THIN CRISPATE sepal tip (pitcheri) vs THICK NONCRISPATE tip (texensis).
For fruit, compare the small ACHENE body with its persistent STYLE/BEAK and whether hairs spread outward.
Do not use flower color, leaf shape or feathery heads as a standalone ID.

visual_comparison.title: Clematis: four sepals, two flower shapes, and feathery styles
visual_comparison.subtitle: These are exact-species photographs already installed in the learner. Each caption states which structure the view supports; no unverified arrows or same-scale flower measurements have been added.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: OPEN four-sepal flowers: DRUMMONDII versus introduced TERNIFLORA — inspect leaflets. NODDING LEATHERY URNS: PITCHERI vs TEXENSIS — inspect SEPAl EDGES and mature achene BEAKS. Feathery fruit alone is NOT enough.

items.label: Old man's beard: OPEN flower
items.image_role: four spreading showy SEPALS and numerous central stamens
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.caption: This is a staminate (male) flower. Look at the pale, spreading SEPALS, not petals, and the abundant stamens in the center. It is not a photograph of a fruit-producing pistillate flower.

items.label: Sweet autumn clematis: many OPEN flowers
items.image_role: many-flowered branched white inflorescence / introduced comparison
items.creator: Σ64
items.caption: Small, open four-sepal flowers crowd into branched flowering sprays. Unlike native old man's beard, this species usually has simpler, entire-edged leaflets; flowers and leaflets should be studied together.

items.label: Purple leatherflower: closed urn
items.image_role: four leathery purple sepals forming a nodding bell
items.creator: Clay Williams
items.caption: Look at a drooping, pitcher-shaped blossom. What looks like joined petals is a close arrangement of four leathery SEPALS. The crucial thin crispate distal sepal margin is not adequately resolved here; specialty close-up pending. Clay Williams image is CC BY-NC 4.0; NONCOMMERCIAL PRIVATE STUDY ONLY, not cleared for public reuse.

items.label: Scarlet leatherflower: long tapered urn
items.image_role: thick noncrispate sepal edges and curved flower tips
items.creator: Mason Brock (Masebrock)
items.caption: Look at the side of the scarlet flower and its four leathery sepals. FNA diagnoses thick, NOT expanded or crispate sepal margins. Photo is an identification portrait, not a verified micromacro of the edge.

items.label: Climbing mechanism: leaf stalks wrap
items.image_role: twining leaf petiole / lobed leaflet context
items.creator: sonnia hill
items.caption: Find the thin LEAF STALK (petiole/petiolule) curved around its support. Clematis climbs with winding leaf stalks, not a separate tendril or adhesive rootlets. The example is from old man's beard.

items.label: Introduced sweet autumn: entire leaflet
items.image_role: simple leaflet edge (unlobed), compound leaf context
items.creator: Alpsdake
items.caption: Look at a single leaflet's mostly smooth, ENTIRE margin. Compare this with the often distinctly cut/lobed individual leaflets of C. drummondii. A single leaflet cannot identify the species on its own.

items.label: Old man's beard: feathery seedheads
items.image_role: dry ACHENE cluster with plumose persistent styles
items.creator: Mike (Commons Pompilid)
items.caption: Each tiny dry fruit is an ACHENE; the long silver feather is its persistent STYLE, not a cottony seed or petal. Both native and introduced white-flowered Clematis may have plumed styles, so combine fruit with flowers and leaves.

items.label: Scarlet leatherflower: vine and bloom
items.image_role: wild growth habit and axillary flower in a habitat view
items.creator: Mason Brock (Masebrock)
items.caption: This wild-plant photograph supplies habit and flower context from Texas. Use it to place the hanging urn on the climbing shoot; fine sepal-edge and plumose achene comparisons require separate macros.
